\chapter{Asking Someone's Age}
\label{ch:ar-asking-age}
\hlchaptermodality{17}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask how old someone is in Arabic and give my own age without using a verb.}

Ask kam ʿumruka? and answer 'ʿumrī ʿishrūna sana' -- age as a noun you possess, no verb anywhere.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\ar{كم} \ar{عمرك؟}]{\ar{كم} \ar{عمرك؟} — asking age with a noun, not a verb}

\label{lesson:AR-C17-kam-umruka}



\begin{quote}
You've seen Romance languages \textbf{have} their years, Germanic languages \textbf{be} their years, and Classical Latin itself use a third construction (\textquotedblleft{}born\textquotedblright{} + accusative of duration). Arabic does something structurally different again: it doesn't use a verb for this at all.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \ar{عمر} — life, lifetime, age}
\textbf{\ar{عمر}} (\emph{ʿumr}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{age, lifetime, life span}\textquotedblright{} — from the root \textbf{\ar{ع}-\ar{م}-\ar{ر}} (\emph{ʿ-m-r}), broadly tied to the idea of \textbf{living, dwelling, flourishing} (the same root behind the personal name \textbf{ʿUmar}, and words for \textquotedblleft{}building, habitation\textquotedblright{}). Age in Arabic isn't something you \emph{have} or \emph{are} — it's expressed as a possessed \textbf{noun}: \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{your} ʿumr,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{my} ʿumr.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \ar{كم} \ar{عمرك؟} — no verb needed}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ar{كم} \ar{عمرك؟}} — \textquotedblleft{}How old are you?\textquotedblright{} (to a man) — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{how much {[}is{]} your} \emph{ʿumr}.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{kam ʿumruka?}) \textbf{\ar{عمري} \ar{عشرون} \ar{سنة}.} — \textquotedblleft{}I am twenty years old.\textquotedblright{} — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{my} \emph{ʿumr} {[}is{]} twenty years.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{ʿumrī ʿishrūna sana}.)
\end{quote}

Notice there's \textbf{no verb \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{} at all} in the present tense here — Arabic simply juxtaposes two nouns (\textquotedblleft{}my age\textquotedblright{} / \textquotedblleft{}twenty years\textquotedblright{}), exactly the way it forms ordinary present-tense sentences without \emph{is/are}. So this is a genuinely \textbf{fourth shape} for the concept: not Romance's \textquotedblleft{}I \textbf{have} twenty years,\textquotedblright{} not Germanic's \textquotedblleft{}I \textbf{am} twenty years {[}old{]},\textquotedblright{} not Latin's \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{born} twenty years {[}so far{]},\textquotedblright{} but \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{my age} {[}is{]} twenty years\textquotedblright{} — age as a possessed noun-quantity, stated without any verb at all.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ʿumr\textquotedblright{} — age, lifetime, life span
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kam ʿumruka?\textquotedblright{} — how old are you? (to a man)
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ʿumrī ʿishrūna sana\textquotedblright{} — my age is twenty years, no verb at all
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\ar{عمر}} literally mean, and what root is it from? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{Age, lifetime}\textquotedblright{} — root \textbf{\ar{ع}-\ar{م}-\ar{ر}}, tied to living/flourishing.) Does Arabic use a verb to state age, the way Romance (\textquotedblleft{}have\textquotedblright{}), Germanic (\textquotedblleft{}be\textquotedblright{}), or Latin (\textquotedblleft{}born\textquotedblright{} + duration) do? (\textbf{No} — it juxtaposes \textquotedblleft{}my age\textquotedblright{} and the number, with no verb needed at all.) What does \textbf{\ar{كم} \ar{عمرك؟}} literally ask? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{How much {[}is{]} your} \emph{ʿumr}?\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bāʾ, nūn, tāʾ, thāʾ · yāʾ · khayr]{The letters that wrote my name}

\label{lesson:AR-R17-the-letters-that-wrote-my-name}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\ar{اسمي}} and \textbf{\ar{خير}} by hand, right to left, without looking below. Both were drawn stroke by stroke in the writing set and neither has been asked for since.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script: one bowl, four letters}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{letter} & \textbf{dots} & \textbf{where it sits} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ar{ب}} \emph{bāʾ} & one below & inside \textbf{\ar{بخير}} \\
\textbf{\ar{ن}} \emph{nūn} & one above & inside \textbf{\ar{أنت}} \\
\textbf{\ar{ت}} \emph{tāʾ} & two above & inside \textbf{\ar{أنت}}, \textbf{\ar{تشرفنا}} \\
\textbf{\ar{ث}} \emph{thāʾ} & three above & — \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

One shallow boat-bowl, drawn the same way every time. Only the dots change, and the dots \textbf{are} the letter. Two of these four build the word for \emph{you}: an \emph{alif} with a hamza seat, then \emph{nūn}, then \emph{tāʾ}.

\subsection*{Script: the letter with three jobs}
\textbf{\ar{ي}} \emph{yāʾ} is the same bowl body with \textbf{two dots below} — a tooth when joined. It does three separate jobs, and you have used all three:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item consonant \textbf{y}, as in \emph{yawm}, a day
  \item the long vowel \textbf{ī}, a seat for the \emph{ee} sound
  \item the suffix \textbf{\ar{ـي}}, glued on to mean \textbf{my}
\end{itemize}

That third job is what turns \textbf{\ar{اسم}} into \textbf{\ar{اسمي}}. Four letters, right to left: \emph{alif · sīn · mīm · yāʾ}.

\subsection*{Script: the marks everyday text leaves off}
The \textbf{ḥarakāt} are three small marks written around a consonant, not letters of their own: \emph{fatḥa} above for \emph{a}, \emph{kasra} below for \emph{i}, \emph{ḍamma} above for \emph{u}. Arabic is an abjad, so ordinary text leaves them out — and one of them carries the whole difference between \textbf{\ar{أنتَ}} and \textbf{\ar{أنتِ}}.

\textbf{Hamza} is not one of them. It writes a real consonant: the glottal catch in the middle of English \emph{uh-oh}. Written alone it is \textbf{\ar{ء}}; riding an \emph{alif} seat it is \textbf{\ar{أ}}, which is how the word for \emph{you} begins.

\subsection*{Script: \ar{خير}, taken apart}
\textbf{\ar{خ}} \emph{khāʾ} belongs to the hook-and-tail family — a rounded hook flowing into a tail that drops below the line, with \textbf{one dot above}. Its plain cousin \textbf{\ar{ح}} has no dot and \textbf{\ar{ج}} takes one below.

Write these out:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{خير}} right to left — \emph{khāʾ} with its dot, into \emph{yāʾ}, then \emph{rā}, and lift
  \item glue \textbf{\ar{بـ}} on the front — \textbf{\ar{بخير}}, its one dot below, joining straight into the \emph{khāʾ}
  \item \textbf{\ar{اسمي}} — \emph{alif · sīn · mīm · yāʾ}
\end{itemize}

Nothing joins after \textbf{\ar{ر}}, which is why the pen lifts there.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name the one feature that separates \textbf{\ar{ب} \ar{ن} \ar{ت} \ar{ث}}. (\textbf{The dots} — one below, one above, two above, three above.) Give \emph{yāʾ}'s three jobs. (\textbf{Consonant y, long vowel ī, the suffix meaning my}.) Say whether hamza is a vowel mark. (\textbf{No} — a glottal stop.) And say what \textbf{\ar{بـ}} adds to \textbf{\ar{خير}}. (\emph{\textbf{In}} — in goodness.)
\end{tcolorbox}
